topic: Open Agent Compat Lab: Deterministic Compatibility for Agent Endpoints

key_points: AgentProbe is a validator + directory that runs a deep protocol assessment over the whole agent stack: MCP (Model Context Protocol), A2A, x402 HTTP-native payments, UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol), and ERC-8004 on-chain agent identity across 14 EVM chains
For MCP it checks spec compliance, tool discovery and transport; for A2A it reads and validates the Agent Card at /.well-known and validates capabilities and identity
Three-step trust model: Discover (by tools or project), Validate (deep protocol assessment of spec/tools/transport/payments), Trust (on-chain signals, deployer history, multi-chain presence)
Only publishes servers that pass — no searchable wall of broken endpoints; a failed endpoint is returned to the operator privately for remediation rather than publicly listed
Explicitly positions itself as a compatibility/validation gate for the emerging 'agent web'
WellKnownMCP builds a cryptographic trust infrastructure for agent discoverability: agents visiting /.well-known/mcp.llmfeed.json discover structured capabilities, auth methods, and business intent
Leverages RFC 8615 (the standard .well-known/ URI) so discovery is deterministic and standards-compliant rather than guessed from pixels
Uses Ed25519 cryptographic signatures, PKI infrastructure and certificate chains so an agent can verify a site is legitimate instead of trusting visually
Measured advantage over traditional sites: 2 seconds vs 30+ seconds discovery (15x faster), ~2,000 vs ~15,000 tokens (7.5x cheaper), 95% vs 70% confidence, plus cryptographic trust verification
Companion projects: LLMCA.org (certification authority), LLMFeedForge.org (visual builder) — a full deterministic discovery + certification stack
A2Apex is a testing/certification/directory layer built on Google's A2A protocol for agent interoperability

Four-step flow: Point (enter agent URL, auto-discover agent card + capabilities), Test (automated compliance suite over the full A2A protocol), Certify (public profile with trust score), List (directory discovery)

Does Agent Card validation (schema compliance vs the A2A spec), live endpoint testing via real JSON-RPC calls with response validation, and security checking (API key, OAuth, JWT auth scheme validation)
Trust scoring: 0-100 score with tiered badges (Gold/Silver/Bronze) built from a running test history
Framing: agents fail silently in production, every framework speaks a different language, and there is no way to verify agent quality — this is the gap a compat lab fills
Defines the Agent Endpoint as the next addressable layer of commercial reality: 'Every business will have one' — the 2026 successor to the 1995 business URL

An endpoint is a four-layer stack: Public Surface (how it's reached — URL, phone/SIP, chat handle, llms.txt), Reasoning Core (LLM, system prompt, persona, guardrails), Tool Belt (MCP servers, REST APIs, webhooks — authority in machine-readable form), System of Record (inventory, contracts, prices, ground truth)
A2A exchange is two-sided: a caller's agent dials a business's agent, and the two resolve the request without a human navigating menus

Deterministic compatibility must therefore cover every layer — not just the transport, but the reasoning core and tool belt, because an endpoint that is fluent but disconnected from its system of record is useless
Discovery already has a directory pattern; the challenge is making an agent reliably dial the right endpoint and get a verifiable, correctly-typed response
Google's A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol is an open standard for agent-to-agent interoperability, published at a2a-protocol.org
The Agent Card is the discovery object (4.4.1): a JSON document at /.well-known/agent-card.json carrying capabilities, skills, providers, interfaces, and an AgentCardSignature for verification
The spec defines operation semantics explicitly for determinism: idempotency (3.3.1), error handling (3.3.2), asynchronous processing (3.3.3), and capability validation (3.3.4)
Agent discovery objects include AgentCard, AgentProvider, AgentCapabilities, AgentSkill, AgentInterface, AgentCardSignature (4.4.1-4.4.7)
Security objects formalize auth: SecurityScheme, APIKeySecurityScheme, HTTPAuthSecurityScheme, OAuth2SecurityScheme, OpenIdConnectSecurityScheme, MutualTlsSecurityScheme (4.5.1-4.5.7)

Section 5 'Protocol Binding Requirements and Interoperability' specifies functional-equivalence requirements and protocol selection — the canonical reference for what a deterministic compat test must verify

stats.fact: A2A Agent Card is discovered deterministically at /.well-known/agent-card.json and includes a verifiable AgentCardSignature
The A2A spec formalizes determinism-critical semantics: idempotency, error handling, asynchronous processing, and capability validation (sections 3.3.1-3.3.4)
WellKnownMCP claims structured MCP discovery is ~15x faster than traditional page scanning (2s vs 30+s) and ~7.5x cheaper in tokens (~2,000 vs ~15,000)
WellKnownMCP uses RFC 8625 (.well-known/ URI) plus Ed25519 signatures / PKI for cryptographic endpoint verification
AgentProbe validates 5 protocol layers per endpoint: MCP, A2A, x402, UCP, and ERC-8007 (on-chain identity across 14 EVM chains)
A2Apex runs live JSON-RPC calls against agent endpoints with response validation plus auth-scheme checks (API key, OAuth, JWT)
A2Apex assigns a 0-100 trust score with tiered Gold/Silver/Bronze badges built from an ongoing automated test history
An Agent Endpoint is a four-layer stack (public surface / reasoning core / tool belt / system of record) — compatibility must be verified at all four layers, not just the callable surface
A2A protocol security is formalized into machine-checkable schemes: APIKey, HTTPAuth, OAuth2, OpenID Connect, and mutual TLS (sections 4.5.1-4.5.7)

angles: Deterministic compatibility means verifying the contract, not just the response: schema-valid Agent Cards, idempotent operations, and reproducible error handling are the testable surface of an endpoint

A compat lab is the trust layer between fragmented agent frameworks: LangChain, AutoGPT, CrewAI, Claude, and Gemini agents all speak different dialects, and there is no vendor-neutral gate that says 'this endpoint works'
The two-layer answer: standards for discovery (RFC 8625 .well-known, Agent Card) plus certification layers (AgentProbe, A2Apex) that turn 'it responds' into 'it is verified compatible'
Cryptographic verification (Ed25519 signatures, PKI, ERC-8007 on-chain identity) is the deterministic upgrade from the old trust-blind model where agents guess from pixels
Compatibility has cost and speed dimensions: structured discovery cuts token cost ~7.5x and discovery time ~15x — a compat lab should benchmark these, not just pass/fail the contract

The four-layer endpoint model (surface / reasoning / tools / system of record) argues that endpoint compatibility is a multi-surface problem: a fluent but ungrounded endpoint is a compatibility failure even when it responds
Auth verification is a first-class compatibility signal: API-key vs OAuth vs mutual-TLS schemes must be validated deterministically before an agent is allowed to dial an endpoint
